name: Visa

header.one_liner: Toll road on global card volume; quality is not in question, but the cost of keeping the banks is rising.
header.thesis: Visa closed fiscal 2026 with 15% net revenue growth and guides fiscal 2027 to low double digit revenue and low double digit to low teens EPS growth. At about 29x fiscal 2027 EPS the market assumes that holds. Client incentives grew 21% in Q4, crossing the engine's 20% tripwire, so the scenario weights tilt toward the bear case and the stance is a position to challenge, not an add.

base.eps_label: FY2027E non-GAAP EPS (year to September 2027): fiscal 2026 $13.27 grown about 12%, the middle of guidance for low double digit to low teens growth
base.rev_label: FY2027E net revenue ($B): fiscal 2026 $45.9B grown about 11%, in line with guidance for low double digit growth

rev_cagr.why: Q4 net revenue grew 13% on 9% payments volume, 14% cross-border volume and 10% more processed transactions; fiscal 2026 grew 15%. Management guides fiscal 2027 net revenue to low double digit growth. The base case assumes about 11% a year, fading slightly over three years.
rev_cagr.source: Visa FQ4 2026 release; FY2027 outlook from the earnings call

margin_end.why: Non-GAAP net margin was about 55% in fiscal 2026 ($25.3B on $45.9B). The base case holds it near 54.5% because opex is guided to grow low double digits, in line with revenue, while client incentives grew 21% in Q4, faster than gross revenue. This is the engine's judgment, not a company number.
margin_end.source: Computed from FQ4 2026 release; FY2027 opex outlook from the call

share_chg.why: Visa repurchased about 61M shares for $20.5B in fiscal 2026, roughly 3% of the count, and has $24.4B of authorisation left. The base case assumes about 2.5% a year as the $2.4B BioCatch purchase and litigation escrow take some cash.
share_chg.source: Visa FQ4 2026 release and call (repurchases, remaining authorisation)

exit_pe.why: Current multiple is about 29x fiscal 2027 EPS and 32x fiscal 2026. The base case assumes a de-rating to 27x as growth settles near ten percent. Bear assumes regulatory or competitive pressure takes it to the low twenties. This is the most disputable number on the page.
exit_pe.source: Engine judgment; current multiple computed from the 13 November close and FY27E EPS

pillars.title: Network effects convert volume into earnings
pillars.claim: Payments volume of +9% and 74.2B processed transactions (+10%) fed net revenue of +13%, because pricing and value-added services grow on top of volume.

evidence.t: Net revenue $12.1B, +13% nominal and constant dollar; fiscal 2026 $45.9B, +15%

pillars.test: Does net revenue growth stay above payments volume growth through fiscal 2027?

pillars.title: Cost growth cooled
pillars.claim: Non-GAAP opex grew 12% in Q4 against 17% in Q3, back below revenue growth. Fiscal 2027 opex is guided to low double digit growth, in line with revenue.

evidence.t: Q4 special items: $469M litigation provision, $282M donation of investments to the Visa Foundation

pillars.test: Does opex growth stay at or below revenue growth in fiscal 2027?

pillars.title: Client incentives are the quiet cost lever
pillars.claim: Incentives of $5.1B grew 21%, up from 18% in Q3 and 16% in Q2, and are now about 30% of gross revenue. They are the price Visa pays to keep issuers on the network, and they are where competitive pressure shows first.

evidence.t: Gross revenue lines: service $5.26B (+14%), data processing $6.2B (+16%), international $4.12B (+8%), other $1.65B (+40%)

pillars.test: Do incentives grow slower than gross revenue in fiscal Q1 2027?

pillars.title: Capital return supports EPS
pillars.claim: A 2.5% to 3% annual share count reduction adds roughly three points to EPS growth, and the dividend rose 16%.

evidence.t: Fiscal 2026 buybacks $20.5B (61M shares); dividends $5.1B; $24.4B authorisation left

pillars.test: Does the buyback pace hold with BioCatch ($2.4B) closing by March 2027?

variant.street: The market pays about 29x fiscal 2027 EPS, which prices a durable low-teens compounder with little regulatory drag.
variant.ours: The engine's base case earns about the hurdle: a high-quality business at a full price. Incentives growing 21% tripped the test we set, so we now weight the bear case at 30% and the bull at 20%. The variant view is that the share Visa pays back to banks, not volume, decides the next leg.
variant.could_be_wrong: If incentive growth was front-loaded renewals and cools in fiscal 2027 while value-added services keep growing 30%, a 29x multiple can persist and the bull case becomes the base case.
variant.would_change_mind: Back to neutral weights if incentives grow slower than gross revenue for two quarters. Negative on two quarters of net revenue growth below 10%.

moat.summary: Two-sided network with issuers and merchants on both sides; fiscal 2026 non-GAAP net margin about 55%.
moat.detail: The existing Porter card (10-K based, FY2025) rates Visa Strong. The fiscal 2026 10-K does not contradict it, but buyer power from issuers shows in incentives growing faster than revenue.

quality.leverage_note: Debt about $22.1B against cash, restricted cash and investments of about $14.8B at 30 September 2026 (third-party tally of the 10-K): modest leverage for a business earning about $30B a year pre-tax.
quality.incentive_note: Incentives to clients grew 21% in Q4 against 13% net revenue growth, the third quarter in a row of acceleration.
checks: Tax rate 18.4% non-GAAP in Q4; fiscal 2027 guided at about 19%
Fiscal 2026 free cash flow about $22.1B against $25.6B of buybacks and dividends (third-party tally); the gap was funded from cash

catalysts.label: Visa fiscal Q1 2027 earnings (date not confirmed; usually late January)
catalysts.note: Guide: net revenue and opex growth low double digits; EPS growth low end of mid-teens.

catalysts.label: BioCatch acquisition ($2.4B cash) expected to close by end of March 2027

tripwires.text: Net revenue growth below 10% in a quarter

tripwires.note: Q2 16%, Q3 18%, Q4 21%. Scenario weights moved to 30% bear, 50% base, 20% bull.

tripwires.text: Opex growth above revenue growth for two quarters
tripwires.note: Q3's gap (opex +17% vs revenue +14%) did not repeat in Q4.

risks: Interchange litigation: the merchant settlement has preliminary court approval (June 2026) but not final approval; routing legislation remains possible with a new Congress in January 2027.
Account-to-account and stablecoin rails taking low-value volume.
Agentic commerce is an opportunity in the company's words, with no revenue disclosed.

lenses.eisman: Look at the incentive line, not the headline: 16%, then 18%, then 21% growth in what Visa pays banks is the number that moves first if the network's pricing power weakens.
lenses.munger: Invert it: what makes Visa a bad investment from here? The price, and banks taking a bigger slice. The business has few ways to fail.
lenses.buffett: A toll road with a 55% net margin is exactly the kind of business he buys, at a price he would call full when the earnings yield is about 3.5% against a 5.15% Treasury.
lenses.hohn: Cost growth cooled to 12% and the dividend rose 16%. Check that the $2.4B BioCatch deal and rising incentives are buying growth rather than defending share.

review.basis: Fiscal 2026 10-K and Q4 release (year to 30 September 2026), the fiscal 2027 outlook from the call, and prices to the 13 November 2026 close; news reviewed to 16 November. Fiscal Q1 2027 reports in late January; this review refreshes after the print.
review.headline: A toll road on global spending with a 55% net margin. Quality is not in question; what Visa pays banks to stay is rising faster than what it earns.
review.model: Visa runs the network that connects card-issuing banks and merchants' banks. It earns a small fee on volume and per transaction, and never lends money.

how_it_earns.v: Fees on payments volume, charged to issuers. Tracks spending.
Per-transaction fees for authorising, clearing and settling, plus value-added services.
Cross-border and currency-conversion fees. Highest margin, tracks travel and e-commerce.
Payments back to banks and merchants to win and keep volume. A contra-revenue line.

mix.note: Revenue only: Visa reports one segment. Shares are of gross revenue before client incentives, which are netted off to reach net revenue.

rows.label: International
rows.driver: Cross-border volume +14%, but revenue only +8% as Visa Direct transfers carry lower fees

rows.label: Client incentives
rows.driver: +21%, faster than gross revenue for a third quarter

callout.label: Value-added services
callout.text: Cuts across the lines above. About $14B in fiscal 2026, up 30% in constant dollars.

review.position: One of two global open-loop networks with Mastercard. Larger by revenue and market value; Mastercard is growing slightly faster.

moat.threat: Regulators and big issuers, not rivals, decide how much of the toll Visa keeps.

what_numbers_say.d: Q4 net revenue +13% on payments volume +9% and transactions +10%. Fiscal 2026 net revenue +15%, the fastest in over 15 years outside the post-pandemic rebound.

what_numbers_say.t: Value-added services are the new engine
what_numbers_say.d: About $14B in fiscal 2026, +30%. Other revenue, where consulting sits, rose 40% to $1.65B in Q4.
Client incentives +21% in Q4 (Q3 +18%, Q2 +16%), about 30% of gross revenue.
Non-GAAP opex +12% in Q4 against net revenue +13%, after +17% in Q3. Fiscal 2027 opex is guided to low double digit growth.

balance.read: Net cash-like leverage. The real liabilities are litigation and settlement guarantees, not debt.
facts: Total debt about $22.1B, down from $25.2B a year earlier
Interchange litigation funded by class B conversion: $469M Q4 provision, $405M escrow deposit in September

flags.flag: Litigation costs sit outside non-GAAP and outside class A
flags.evidence: $469M of Q4 interchange provisions, excluded from non-GAAP. They are funded by reducing class B conversion rates, so class A EPS is unaffected.
Cross-border volume +14% but international transaction revenue only +8% in Q4, partly because lower-fee Visa Direct transfers are a growing share.
New Brazilian rules require Visa to extend settlement guarantees to sellers; Visa expects settlement exposure to increase.

forecast_basis.rev_cagr: Guidance-anchored: fiscal 2027 low double digits, fading toward 10%
forecast_basis.margin_end: Trend: held flat because opex is guided to grow with revenue
forecast_basis.share_chg: Trend: about 2.5% a year from buybacks
forecast_basis.exit_pe: Judgment: modest de-rating from about 29x as growth settles

base.story: Volume grows high single digits, pricing and services add a few points, buybacks add three; EPS compounds low teens, as guided for fiscal 2027.
base.needs: No change to US interchange or routing rules

downside.story: Routing mandates or an interchange settlement cut the toll; incentives rise to defend share; the multiple falls toward the low twenties.
downside.needs: Routing legislation passes, or incentives keep growing above 20%

upside.story: Value-added services and agentic commerce become a second engine; growth holds at 12% and the multiple stays near 30x.
upside.needs: Value-added services keep growing about 30% with margins intact

risks.how: Routing mandates or interchange limits let merchants send transactions to cheaper networks. The merchant settlement awaits final approval, and routing bills could return in the new Congress.
risks.watch: Service revenue per dollar of volume

risks.cause: Big banks demand a bigger share
risks.how: Issuers are concentrated and can switch networks at renewal. Incentives grew 21% in Q4, the fastest of the year.
International fees are the highest-margin line. Revenue grew only 8% on 14% volume in Q4 as lower-fee transfers grew.
Real-time account-to-account systems (Pix, UPI) and stablecoins bypass cards, starting with small transactions in emerging markets.
Opex growth cooled to 12% in Q4, but World Cup marketing and the BioCatch deal add cost in fiscal 2027.

peer_read.why_premium: Visa has the highest EBITDA margin in the group, the largest network, and no credit risk. Mastercard earns more on its smaller capital base.
peer_read.why_not: Mastercard grows faster on consensus and trades at a slightly lower forward EV/EBITDA, so Visa's premium over its closest twin is hard to justify on growth alone.
peer_read.peers_note: American Express is a lender, so it is compared on P/E only. PayPal trades on a very different multiple because its growth and margins are lower.

questions: Are rising incentives a cost of growth or a sign of weakening bargaining power?
Why did cross-border revenue grow at half the rate of cross-border volume?
Would you pay a premium to Mastercard for slower growth?

review.title: A full toll, and the banks want more
review.lead: We rate Visa {rating} with a 12-month target of {pt} ({upside} upside, {ret} total return against a cost of equity of {hurdle}). Fiscal 2026 was Visa's strongest year in over a decade, but client incentives grew 21% in Q4, the shares trade at a premium to Mastercard, and our next-year EPS is {vs_cons} consensus.
review.call_reason: Great business, full price, rising cost of share: the target implies {ret} over 12 months against a cost of equity of {hurdle}.

arguments.label: Growth
arguments.text: Net revenue grew 13% in Q4 and 15% in fiscal 2026 on 9% payments volume growth and 10% more transactions. Management guides fiscal 2027 to low double digit revenue growth and low double digit to low teens EPS growth.

arguments.label: Moat
arguments.text: A two-sided network accepted almost everywhere and embedded with banks and merchants. Regulators and large issuers, not rival networks, decide how much of the toll Visa keeps, and incentives show the issuers pushing.

arguments.label: Profitability
arguments.text: Margins lead the industry and cost growth cooled to 12% in Q4, back below revenue growth. The pressure point is client incentives, up 21% and now about 30% of gross revenue.

arguments.label: Capital
arguments.text: Buybacks of $20.5B in fiscal 2026 cut the share count by about 3%, and the dividend rose 16%. The real liabilities are interchange litigation, funded through the class B shares, and a new settlement guarantee in Brazil.

arguments.label: Valuation
arguments.text: {peer_line} Mastercard is expected to grow faster at a slightly lower multiple.

thesis_long: Visa earns a small fee on a very large and steadily growing base of card spending, never lends money, and converts more than half of net revenue into net income. Fiscal 2026 net revenue grew 15% and EPS 16%, and management guides another year of low double digit growth. Quality is not in question.

The question is what it is worth, and who keeps the toll. Client incentives grew 16%, 18% and 21% in the last three quarters, faster than gross revenue each time; cross-border revenue grew 8% on 14% volume; and Visa still trades at a premium to Mastercard on forward EV/EBITDA despite slower consensus growth. The merchant settlement awaits final approval, and routing legislation could return with a new Congress in January 2027.

Our base case keeps growth near 11% with flat margins and steady buybacks, which supports low-teens EPS growth and a base-case 12-month return a few points above the cost of equity. Incentives crossing 20% tripped the test we set, so we weight the downside more heavily than before, and on those weights the expected return is about the hurdle. The upside case needs value-added services to keep growing 30%; the downside is routing legislation or rising incentives cutting the toll. Two quarters of incentives growing slower than gross revenue would bring us back to neutral.

upside_risks.how: Value-added services of about $14B grew 30% in fiscal 2026. Sustained at core-network margins, they would lift growth and support a premium to Mastercard.
Final approval of the merchant settlement on current terms would remove the main bear argument.
